name: Battle of Stalingrad
info: The Soviet Union defeated Germany and its Axis allies at Stalingrad on the Volga between 1942 and 1943; the German 6th Army was encircled and surrendered, and the strategic initiative on the Eastern Front passed to the Red Army.

facts.date: 17 July 1942 (first clash on the approaches) to 2 February 1943; the German offensive on the city began on 23 August 1942
facts.place: The city of Stalingrad (now Volgograd) on the Volga and the steppe around it, in southern Russia
facts.sides: The Soviet Union (five armies in and around the city, under commanders including Chuikov and Yeryomenko, with nine more in the counteroffensive) against Germany and its Axis allies: the 6th Army under Paulus and the 4th Panzer Army under Hoth of Army Group B under Weichs, with Romanian, Italian, Hungarian and Croatian forces; about 330,000 Axis personnel were encircled
facts.outcome: The Soviet counteroffensive encircled the German 6th Army, which surrendered on 2 February 1943 with around 91,000 prisoners taken.

t: Germany went for Stalingrad as part of a summer offensive aimed at the Caucasus oil fields, and the city became a matter of prestige for both Hitler and Stalin.
After three months of house-to-house fighting in which the Germans took 90% of the ruined city, the Red Army encircled the 6th Army from its flanks on 19 to 23 November 1942.
Casualty figures are widely disputed, with Axis estimates from 800,000 to 1,500,000 and Soviet archival totals of over a million, and most German prisoners died in captivity.
dyk: Between 23 and 26 August 1942 Soviet reports record 955 people killed and 1,181 wounded in the bombing, while estimates of civilian dead from the bombing reach 40,000 or 70,000, though these may be exaggerated.
ev: Case Blue, the German summer offensive, opens on 28 June
German forces first clash with the Stalingrad Front on 17 July in the bend of the Don
The 6th Army reaches the outskirts on 23 August and Luftflotte 4 bombs the city
The battle for the city itself begins on 13 September
On 14 October a German assault reaches the Volga at the tractor factory and splits the 62nd Army

sections.background:
By the spring of 1942 the German armed forces had captured vast territories of the Soviet Union, including Ukraine, Belarus and the Baltic republics, but had not defeated it in a single campaign. Germany's fuel supplies had dwindled, and Hitler decided that the summer campaign of 1942 would aim at the southern Soviet Union and the oil fields of the Caucasus. Stalingrad was one of the largest industrial centres of the Soviet Union and a transport hub on the Volga. Controlling it would provide a supply route for the Caucasus campaign and prevent Soviet shipments along the river. The city also bore the name of Joseph Stalin, the Soviet leader.

Stalin was convinced that the main German attack would fall on Moscow. A Soviet offensive from the Izyum salient south of Kharkov began on 12 May and ended in a German encirclement that destroyed much of the Soviet force, leaving the Red Army vulnerable to the summer offensive. Case Blue opened on 28 June 1942. Hitler divided the army group: Army Group A under Wilhelm List advanced towards the Caucasus, and Army Group B under Maximilian von Weichs, with Friedrich Paulus's 6th Army and Hermann Hoth's 4th Panzer Army, moved east towards the Volga and Stalingrad. On 23 July Hitler widened the objectives to include occupying the city. He is recorded as ordering that after its capture all male citizens be killed and women and children deported, because of their "thoroughly communistic" nature. By the end of July Soviet forces had been pushed back across the Don.
sections.forces:
The Red Army deployed five armies in and around the city (the 28th, 51st, 57th, 62nd and 64th). The 62nd Army under Vasiliy Chuikov was formed on 11 September and told to hold the city. When it fell back into the city on 12 September it had been reduced to 90 tanks, 700 mortars and just 20,000 personnel. Stalin's Order No. 227 of 27 July subjected commanders who ordered unauthorised retreats to military tribunal, and blocking detachments were posted behind Red Army units. At the start of the battle 75,000 women and girls from the Stalingrad area who had finished military or medical training were to serve in it.

On the Axis side the 6th Army and 4th Panzer Army of Army Group B attacked the city, supported by Luftflotte 4 under Wolfram von Richthofen, which began with 1,600 aircraft, of which 1,155 were operational. The Soviet air force was left with 192 serviceable aircraft by the end of August, 57 of them fighters. Italian, Hungarian and Romanian armies guarded the northern flank along the Don and the Romanian 4th Army the southern; the Hungarian 2nd Army held 200 km of front thinly. The 369th (Croatian) Reinforced Infantry Regiment was the only non-German unit selected to enter the city in the assault. No overall figure for the Axis forces at the start is given.

Chuikov's tactic was to "hug" the enemy, keeping Soviet positions as close as possible to German ones so that German aircraft and artillery could not strike without risking their own men. Soviet assault groups of 20 to 50 men moved through sewers and broke through walls.
sections.course:
German forces first clashed with the Stalingrad Front on 17 July in the bend of the Don. On 23 August the 6th Army and elements of the 4th Panzer Army launched their offensive, and Luftflotte 4 dropped some 1,000 tons of bombs; at least 90% of the city's housing stock was destroyed. The battle for the city itself began on 13 September. Mamayev Kurgan changed hands many times, and small groups held positions such as the grain elevator and Pavlov's House. By 27 September the Germans held the south of the city, the Soviets the centre and north and the ferries across the Volga.

After 27 September the fighting moved to the factory district. On 14 October, which Chuikov considered the worst day of the battle, a German assault reached the tractor factory and the Volga and split the 62nd Army in two; Hitler suspended all other operations on the Eastern Front. By November the Germans held 90% of the city, with Soviet forces in narrow pockets on the west bank. From 21 August to 20 November the 6th Army lost 60,548 men (12,782 killed, 45,545 wounded and 2,221 missing).

On 19 November the Red Army launched Operation Uranus, overrunning the Romanian 3rd Army on the 6th Army's northern flank; a second thrust on 20 November struck the Romanian 4th Army Corps to the south. The two met at Kalach on 23 November and sealed the ring. About 330,000 Axis personnel were trapped, among them Germans, Romanians, Italians and Croatians, and between 40,000 and 65,000 Hilfswillige ("Hiwis"), volunteer auxiliaries recruited from Soviet prisoners and civilians.
sections.aftermath:
Hitler forbade a breakout and relied on an airlift, which delivered only 105 tons a day against the 750 tons needed. Operation Winter Storm, Manstein's relief attempt, came within 48 km of the 6th Army by 18 December and was abandoned on 23 December. On 7 January 1943 the Soviet command offered Paulus terms, including safety for prisoners, medical care and repatriation after the war; Paulus asked permission to surrender and Hitler refused. After Operation Koltso began on 10 January the airfields were lost, and on 30 January Hitler made Paulus a field marshal. The southern pocket collapsed on 31 January, and the northern one under Karl Strecker surrendered on 2 February.

Around 91,000 exhausted, ill, wounded and starving prisoners were taken, including 22 generals. Most died. Weakened by disease, starvation and lack of medical care during the encirclement, they were sent on forced marches to camps and later to labour camps across the Soviet Union. Some 35,000 were sent on transports, of which 17,000 did not survive. The last of the 5,000 to 6,000 survivors were repatriated to West Germany in 1955.

Both sides disregarded civilians. German troops who reached a hospital for mentally handicapped children shot all the patients aged ten to fourteen, and Soviet machine-gun fire killed Russian women sheltering during the fighting at the Barrikady settlement. About 99% of the city was destroyed. After the battle a quick census found 1,515 people; Antony Beevor notes a census that counted 9,796 civilians, 994 of them children.
sections.sources:
The battle is known from both armies' records and from what was written at the time. It is documented in letters and journals found on German dead, the memoirs of Chuikov and Zhukov, and the first-hand report of Alexander Werth, who visited the city on 3 to 5 February 1943. Omer Bartov studied 11,237 letters sent by soldiers inside the city between 20 December 1942 and 16 January 1943, and Soviet NKVD and Don Front reports survive.

The losses are disputed. For the Axis, estimates range from 800,000 to 1,500,000 casualties (killed, wounded or captured): Peter H. Wilson gives 800,000 including the Romanians, and the multivolume Great Patriotic War history and Geoffrey Jukes give up to 1.5 million, which has been called an overestimate. For the Soviet Union, archival figures give 1,129,619 casualties (478,741 killed or missing and 650,878 wounded or sick); a later revision gives 1,347,214. Boris Sokolov puts the dead at over two million, but many Russian historians regard his figures as unreliable.

Civilian losses are also uncertain. Soviet reports give 955 killed and 1,181 wounded between 23 and 26 August, while estimates of civilians killed by the bombing reach 40,000 or 70,000, which may be exaggerated. Incomplete party archives record 42,754 residents dead; Tatyana Pavlova calculates 185,232 dead of 710,000 inhabitants, or 235,232 with the rural areas. Historians also disagree over Soviet coercion. Beevor claims 13,500 Soviet soldiers were executed, which has been disputed; Richard Overy warns against reducing the Soviet effort to coercion.
sections.legacy:
Stalingrad ended Germany's 1942 summer offensive and passed the strategic initiative on the Eastern Front to the Soviet Union. It is generally regarded as the turning point of the war in Europe; a 1989 quantitative study and a 2004 analysis reached the same conclusion, and Hitler himself blamed Stalingrad for Germany's impending doom in a speech on 9 November 1944. The German public was told of the defeat at the end of January 1943, and on 18 February Joseph Goebbels gave his Sportpalast speech calling for total war.

In the Soviet Union confidence in victory rose, and Stalin was made a Marshal of the Soviet Union. The news was said to have inspired resistance movements in occupied Europe. A ceremonial Sword of Stalingrad was forged for King George VI and given to Stalin by Winston Churchill at the Tehran Conference. Stalingrad was awarded the title Hero City in 1945, and The Motherland Calls was erected on Mamayev Kurgan in 1967. In post-Soviet Russia the victory is among the Days of Military Honour; Volgograd held a parade on 2 February 2013, and parades have been held there since. Every year hundreds of bodies of soldiers are recovered and reburied in cemeteries at Mamayev Kurgan or Rossoshka.

Geoffrey Roberts calls it the biggest and most traumatic defeat in German military history, and Glantz and others describe it as the most brutal clash of the war. Joe Castillo argues that Stalin's leadership and Order No. 227 turned the battle into a deliberate bloodbath for Soviet troops.

summary: At Stalingrad, from the summer of 1942 to 2 February 1943, German and Axis forces fought the Red Army for a ruined city on the Volga until the Soviet counteroffensive encircled the 6th Army. Casualty figures are uncertain, civilians and prisoners died in great numbers, and the battle is generally seen as the war's turning point in Europe.
notes: Start date: the source has no infobox date; 17 July 1942 is its first clash with the Stalingrad Front and 2 February 1943 the 6th Army's capitulation. The German offensive on the city itself began on 23 August.

The source's Axis order of battle is empty, so no overall Axis strength at the start is given; the only strengths are Luftflotte 4's aircraft, the 62nd Army on 12 September and the encircled 330,000 (the source also says about 210,000 were in the pocket on 19 November with 50,000 outside, which does not match 330,000, so only the 330,000 is used).

Casualties: the source gives many incompatible figures (Axis 800,000 to 1,500,000; Soviet 1,129,619 archival and 1,347,214 revised; civilians 42,754 to 235,232). I gave ranges with attributions and no single figure. The source also quotes totals of over a million to over three million dead and the Roberts, Hanson and Hellbeck superlatives; I left the superlatives out.

Left out: Hitler's wish that civilians be killed is stated in the source as his order; I wrote 'is recorded as ordering'. Left out for lack of space: Zaytsev, Pavlov's House detail, the women's air regiments, the Luftwaffe's own losses, Operation Little Saturn, the Beevor-versus-Overy detail on terror beyond one sentence, the claim of Kenneth Alibek about tularemia.
The 'Stalin is said to have prevented civilians from leaving' sentence was cut; it is hedged in the source ('It has been said').
The source's claim that Stalingrad 'saved European civilisation' (Daily Telegraph) and the Kersaudy and Delong remarks were left out as opinion.
